CARDIFF, Nov 14 : Wales pulled off one of rugby’s biggest upsets, ending a 73-year winless sequence against New Zealand to beat the All Blacks 35-28 in the Nations Championship on Saturday. They outscored the visitors five tries to four to end a 34-match winning streak for New Zealand in fixtures between the teams. Wales last won against the All Blacks in 1953 and have slumped to some of their worst results in recent years but produced a defensive performance for the ages to shade the Kiwis. They caught the visitors cold with two early tries and two more at the start of the second half, and heroic Welsh defence resisted waves of New Zealand attacks in the closing stages to hold on for a famous victory.

(Writing by Mark Gleeson in Cape Town; Editing by Ed Osmond)

Source: Reuters

GENOA, Italy, Nov 14 : Italy came close but ultimately fell to another Nations Championship loss against Argentina on Saturday, with head coach Gonzalo Quesada left lamenting the errors and missed opportunities which cost his side. The final seconds of the match summed up Italy's afternoon in Genoa, putting themselves in a position to beat Argentina but letting the chance slip away in a 19-14 defeat. With the clock in the red, Italy were awarded a penalty. Paolo Garbisi went for touch in the corner, but the flyhalf overhit his kick and the Italians fell to a sixth consecutive defeat. Quesada's lineout coach, former Italy great Sergio Parisse, shook his head ruefully in the stands, and the two Argentine-born men looked increasingly frustrated throughout the match.

"Knowing that, after all the work we put in together during the week, we could have beaten Argentina with 30 seconds left, and that it was in our hands, hurts," Quesada told reporters. "We had the tools and the opportunity to win, but we let it slip away. We are still missing something, we need to be more solid." Italy failed to capitalise time and again on Argentine ill-discipline, with the Pumas having three players yellow carded. Captain Giacomo Nicotera believes their shortcomings extended beyond an inability to exploit numerical advantage. "It was a very messy game, with two teams going at each other with great intensity," Nicotera said. "My feeling is that even when the numbers were level, there were moments when we could have managed possession better, stayed organised and maintained control of the game, putting them under pressure. "That's something we'll have to review and analyse." This defeat will be one that haunts Quesada, and a loss he will certainly analyse before taking on Fiji next weekend. "I like the fact that the expectations around this team are that it should win," Quesada said. "I get angry when we give things away and those mistakes are entirely down to ourselves. "From where I sat, the feeling was that we could have controlled the game better and put them under pressure. It's one of those matches that I need to watch again before getting back to work."

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Nov 14 : Chelsea handed champions Manchester City their first defeat of the Women's Super League season on Saturday, beating their title rivals 1-0 to climb above them into top spot in the table. Chelsea have 26 points from 10 matches, one ahead of second-placed City after 10 games. The decisive moment came in first-half stoppage time when Sandy Baltimore produced a moment of brilliance, collecting a pass on the right side of the penalty area before turning and rifling an unstoppable shot above goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita. "I think just the intensity is a lot better," Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh told the BBC. "And you could see today, I think we started a bit slow but after that most first and second balls were ours and I think that's what wins you games."

City's hopes of preserving their unbeaten record suffered a further blow in the 75th minute when Yamashita was sent off after racing well outside her area and clattering Alyssa Thompson as the Chelsea forward ran through on goal. Eartha Cumings replaced her as City played the closing stages with 10 players. Chelsea's Aggie Beever-Jones struck the crossbar with a free kick in the second half but the hosts held on for the victory. "I think (top spot) is kind of what Chelsea have been used to for so long but, yeah, it's a nice feeling," Walsh said. "We're in a better place than we were last year, it's a good feeling. We've got one more game before the international break, and we need to finish strong, but we're in a good place, we're confident, and the team's really happy." Chelsea next visit Paris St Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday. Manchester United continued their solid start with a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace with goals from captain Maya Le Tissier and Elisabeth Terland. Le Tissier celebrated her 150th United appearance in memorable fashion in the 18th minute, stepping out from defence to win possession before unleashing a superb long-range effort into the bottom corner of the net. United sealed the points in the 65th when Jess Park collected her second assist of the afternoon, threading a precise pass into the box for Terland, who calmly beat the goalkeeper for her third WSL goal of the season. The win leaves United provisionally fourth on 18 points.

Source: Reuters

GENOA, Italy, Nov 14 : Argentina beat Italy 19-14 on Saturday in a Nations Championship meeting short on quality and high on errors which condemned the hosts to their fifth defeat in five matches in the competition. Italy took an early lead through Monty Ioane's try, converted by Tommaso Allan, but Argentina, who were down to 14 men, levelled just before halftime, with hooker Bautista Bernasconi going over and Tomas Albornoz adding the conversion. Rodrigo Isgro's try in the 55th minute put Argentina ahead and five minutes later Mateo Carreras extended the lead when he went over for the visitors, with Albornoz converting. A penalty try for Italy set up a grandstand finish but Argentina held on for their 10th straight win over the Italians.

Argentina earned their second victory of the competition and are on 11 points, third in the Southern Hemisphere standings, three points ahead of Australia, who visit Scotland on Sunday. Italy earned a losing bonus point, their first of the competition, but will finish bottom of the Northern Hemisphere group. Both sides came into the contest low on confidence and in need of not only victory, but a much-improved performance. Argentina lost 42-12 to Ireland a week ago, while Italy were thumped 66-7 by South Africa in Turin. BRIGHT START The Italian fans suffered through a dominant Springbok performance last week, especially a first half which was all one-way traffic, but this time around the hosts started brightly in Genoa with a fifth-minute try. Leonardo Marin's kick through on the wing bounced up perfectly for Ioane to go over in the corner. That move followed an Italian penalty won at the scrum, and Argentina were penalised twice more in the first half for collapsing. Allan missed a penalty from inside his own half, and Italy continually failed to capitalise on Argentine ill-discipline. After kicking two penalties into the corner, Italy lost their lineout close to the line. Albornoz was sent to the sin-bin just before the half-hour mark but Argentina then had their best spell and Bernasconi's try from a lineout drive was converted by the flyhalf, back on the pitch just in time for the kick. Argentina continued to make plenty of entries into the Italian 22 after the break, but errors let them down until they managed to hold firm in the scrum and worked the ball to the other side for Isgro to put them ahead. Italy lost Enoch Opoku Gyamfi to a yellow card for too many penalties and Argentina pounced immediately with Carreras' try. Argentina's Joel Sclavi was yellow carded, and Efrain Elias quickly followed suit when Italy were awarded a penalty try with 15 minutes remaining but their late pressure went unrewarded. Gonzalo Quesada's Italy will hope to finish off in style next Saturday when they host Fiji in Udine, the only other winless side in the competition, and the pair are likely to meet on finals weekend in the 11th-place final. Argentina travel to Paris next weekend to take on France, who top the Northern Hemisphere standings.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LEVI, Finland, Nov 14 : Germany's Emma Aicher claimed the first women's World Cup slalom of the season on Saturday, turning her opening-run lead into a dominant victory to secure the first slalom win of her career. Aicher, who turned 23 on Friday, had a 0.36-second advantage after the first run and looked comfortable in extending her advantage in the second run on the Levi Black course to finish with a combined time of one minute 52.62 seconds. She finished 0.43 seconds ahead of Albania's Lara Colturi, while Austria's Katharina Truppe climbed from fifth after the first run to complete the podium, 0.50 behind the winner. The victory adds slalom to Aicher's growing World Cup resume after previous wins in downhill and super-G.

"It's a good birthday present," Aicher said. "I like Levi, it was my first (slalom) podium (last year), first win in slalom (this year), so it means a lot to be here. My whole family is here as well, so it's really nice to be able to ski the way I want when they are here. "I'm happy with how I skied in both rounds. There's still a few things I could do better but, overall, I'm happy." Colturi, 19, made the ninth World Cup podium of her career but is still searching for her first World Cup win. Croatia's Zrinka Ljutic, third after the opening run, slipped to fourth. Another major storyline was the return to the discipline of Slovakia's 31-year-old Petra Vlhova, who finished 16th in her first World Cup slalom since January 2024. The six-times Levi winner qualified for the second run in 14th place and showed flashes of her former speed. Vlhova, who came back to the World Cup circuit in the giant slalom at Solden last month, was seriously injured in January 2024 when she fell in that event on home snow in Jasna and tore knee ligaments. She underwent two surgical operations. The season-opening slalom was contested without reigning discipline champion Mikaela Shiffrin, who won nine of the 10 World Cup slaloms last winter. The American plans to begin her slalom campaign at Killington on November 29. Winners of the Levi races receive a live Lapland reindeer as part of their prize, a tradition started in 2013.

Source: Reuters

MANILA: ASEAN is not relaxing its approach to Myanmar under its Five-Point Consensus, though proposals concerning the country's participation in high-level meetings remain under discussion, the bloc's special envoy on Myanmar said on Saturday (Nov 14). The Five-Point Consensus is ASEAN's main framework for responding to the crisis in Myanmar after a military coup there in 2021. It calls, among other things, for an immediate end to violence and the launch of constructive dialogue among all parties, and offers ASEAN mediation and humanitarian assistance. ASEAN is under increasing pressure ahead of a summit of its leaders in Manila that starts on Sunday to ease a five-year ban on Myanmar's military-backed leaders attending high-level meetings. Thailand and several other members have stepped up engagement with Myanmar despite its ongoing civil war. ASEAN special envoy and Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said a draft review of the Five-Point Consensus was still under negotiation and that "a number of proposals" would be presented to the ASEAN leaders.

"To answer you bluntly, there is no easing (of the approach to Myanmar). There is still the Five-Point Consensus," Lazaro told a press conference, when asked whether the review could lead to adjustments to restrictions on Myanmar's political leadership.

ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus

Following a 2021 military coup , ASEAN has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.  During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar. The five points are: First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint. Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people. Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN. Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre. Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.

Collapse Expand

Asked about Thailand's call to allow Myanmar's foreign minister to participate in meetings of ASEAN foreign ministers, Lazaro said it remained under discussion, but no decision had been made to allow the minister to take Myanmar's seat. "It's still there on the table. It's still a subject of discussion," she said. Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations are set to review their decision to exclude Myanmar when they meet in Manila from Nov 15 to Nov 17.

FAST

WASHINGTON, Nov 14 : NASA's Voyager 1 has already traveled farther than any other spacecraft from Earth since its launch in 1977. The probe, which exited our solar system years ago and is journeying through interstellar space, is now on the cusp of a remarkable milestone — traversing a light-day, the distance light travels in 24 hours. A light-day is about 16 billion miles (26 billion km). The US space agency said Voyager 1, flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph) through the virtual vacuum of space, will reach that distance from Earth on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET (1016 GMT). The robotic spacecraft has the distinction of being the most distant human-made object. "I view it as an engineering milestone, marking the amazing longevity of Voyager 1 — and also an engineering achievement to be able to communicate with Voyager 1 at its distance," said astrophysicist Alan Cummings, a senior research scientist in the Space Radiation Laboratory at Caltech who has been a Voyager program scientist since 1973. A light-year may be a more familiar concept for many people, a metric used for vast cosmic distances. It is the distance a particle of light, called a photon, travels in a year — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km). For instance, the closest stars beyond our solar system are the three that make up the Alpha Centauri system, about 4.24 light-years away.

TWIN SPACECRAFT Voyager 1 and twin spacecraft Voyager 2 were launched 49 years ago, exploring planets in the outer solar system before continuing onward. Voyager 1 was carried into space on September 5, 1977, atop a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida 16 days after the launch of Voyager 2, but overtook its twin within months. "Voyager 1 returned a wealth of new information about Jupiter and Saturn, and their moons," Cummings said. It discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two previously undetected Jovian moons, Thebe and Metis. It then spotted five new moons around Saturn as well as a ring called the G-ring. "Voyager 2 took a different path through the solar system after they launched in 1977, in order to visit Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is on pace to be one light-day away from Earth in nine more years, in November 2035," Cummings said. Voyager 1 crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, and entered interstellar space in 2012, continuing to collect data.  "It was the first spacecraft to report the energy spectra of galactic cosmic rays (fast-moving energetic particles) at low energies. Those energetic particles are not observable inside the heliosphere because of the push-back by the solar wind. This was the holy grail of low-energy cosmic ray physics," said Cummings, an expert in cosmic rays. Voyager 2 entered interstellar space in 2018. 'THE BACKBONE OF MY CAREER' Cummings became part of the Voyager scientific team by accident after a balloon-borne experiment concerning cosmic rays that was the basis of his Caltech doctoral thesis failed to land in northern Canada as planned. "It went around the world a time and a half, and was eventually captured by the Soviet Union. It landed apparently without the benefit of the parachute and was essentially destroyed," Cummings said. "It was decided that the experiment was finished, and I was offered a job on the Voyager Cosmic Ray Subsystem (instrument) fairly soon after it began development in 1973. The loss of the balloon was lucky for me as the Voyager mission has been the backbone of my career. I've been working on it and analyzing data from it for 53 years," Cummings said. He joined the Voyager team at age 29 and is now 82. Both Voyagers carry a Golden Record, a device intended to communicate Earth's story to any intelligent extraterrestrial beings who may encounter the spacecraft. The phonograph record, a 12-inch (30.5-cm) gold-plated copper disk, contains various images and sounds to convey our planet's culture. It features music like rocker Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Beethoven's Fifth Symphony and Aboriginal songs from Australia, as well as spoken greetings in 55 languages and instructions for locating Earth. Some experts have subsequently questioned the wisdom of providing directions to our planet, in case covetous hostile beings come across the Golden Record. "I've heard that concern a little over the years but I never worried about it. It's pretty unlikely the aliens will find it," Cummings said.

Source: Reuters
